unit.title: Bonds and fixed income
unit.description: How a bond works, its yield, the effect of interest rates and the risk of default

texts: Lend or buy into the business
Irene
Irene is opening her second bakery and needs money.
I need €1,000. I've got two offers for you.
Either you lend it to me: I pay you 3 % a year and give it back in 5 years.
Or you buy into the business and take a share of the profits, if there are any.
If you lend it to her, what do you get?
€30 a year and my €1,000 back at the end
That's a **bond**! Five €30 coupons plus the face value: **€1,150**.
A share of the bakery's profits
That's buying into the business, like with a **share**. When you lend, you get what was agreed.
It depends on how the bakery does
Only if it goes bust. If it does well or just so-so, you get what was agreed.
Lending: you earn a **coupon** and, at **maturity**, you get the **face value** back.
Bond or share?
With a share you **own** a little piece of the company; with a bond you **lend** it money. Which one does each feature belong to?
Bond: you lend
Share: you own
Has a maturity date
The loan ends on an agreed date and you get the face value back.
Makes you a part-owner of the company
With shares you own a slice of it, with a vote at the general meeting.
Pays a coupon agreed from the start
That's why it's called fixed income: what you're paid is agreed.
You earn more if the company does really well
Shareholders share in the success; bondholders get the same either way.
If the company goes bust, you get paid first
Creditors get paid first; shareholders, last.
Spanish Treasury bills, bonds and obligations
They're government debt: you lend the state money over different terms.
Sort all six features.
With a bond you're a **lender**: you get what was agreed and, if there's a bankruptcy, you're paid before shareholders. That's why it's called **fixed income**.
Hint: are you lending money or buying a piece of the business?
Sort each feature
What bonds are for
Real data from 2008 to 2025: you start with **€10,000**, all in US shares. Move some into bonds and see what changes.
US shares (S&P 500)
US bonds
Gold
If you move some of your shares into bonds, what do you think happens?
You earn more and fall less
You fall less, but end up with less
Nothing changes
Bonds tend to move less than shares: they **cushion** the falls, but over the long run they return less.
Add bonds until the worst fall is no more than 30 %.

With 40 % in bonds, the worst fall drops from 46 % to 28 %, in exchange for ending up with €42,007 instead of €69,328. Bonds **cushion** falls, though not always: in 2022 they fell at the same time as shares.
Look at that fall: 2008 and 2009 really hurt.
Very calm… but look how much less you end up with.
That's it! Fewer scares along the way.
Move some of your shares into bonds

steps.title: Fixed, but not frozen
steps.body:
In Spain, the Treasury issues **bills** (letras, up to 12 months), **bonds** (bonos, 2 to 5 years) and **obligations** (obligaciones, over 5). Companies issue corporate bonds, which usually pay more because they're riskier.

The coupon is fixed, but the bond's **price** changes every day. If you hold it to maturity, you get what was agreed (if the issuer pays). If you sell it earlier, you can make or lose money.
steps.key: A bond is a loan: you earn interest and get your money back at maturity, as long as the issuer can pay.
steps.tip: Share = being an owner. Bond = being a lender.

texts: A bond at €960
A **€1,000** bond with a 4 % coupon matures in a year. Its price depends on the **market interest rate**.
You buy it for €960. What return do you get if you hold it to the end?
4 %, what the coupon says
Quite a bit more than 4 %
Less than 4 %
You get €40 in coupon and €1,000 back for something that cost you €960: you make **€80 on €960**, or 8.33 %.
Find the market rate at which the bond is worth about €960.
That rate is the **YTM** (yield to maturity): what the bond returns if you hold it to maturity, 8.33 % here. If you buy it below €1,000, the YTM is higher than the coupon.
This bond matures in 1 year: leave the term at 1.
You've gone too far: bring the rate down a bit.
There! At that rate, the bond is worth €960.
Raise the market interest rate
The misleading coupon
Dani
Look at these two bonds. Same issuer, and both mature in a year.
Bond A: 6 % coupon, costs €1,030 (quoted «at 103»). Bond B: 2 % coupon, costs €990 («at 99»).
I'm going for A, it pays three times as much.
Which one returns more to maturity?
A: its coupon is three times bigger
It gets €60, but loses €30 at maturity: about **2.91 %**.
B: you buy it below 100
Nice! €20 of coupon and €10 of difference: about **3.03 %**, more than A.
They return exactly the same
They're close, but B returns a little more: 3.03 % versus 2.91 %.
To compare bonds, it's the **YTM** that counts, not the coupon.

steps.title: Three kinds of yield
steps.body:
Bonds are quoted as a **% of face value**: «at 96» means €960 for every €1,000.

• **Coupon:** on the face value. €40 on €1,000 = 4 %.
• **Current yield:** coupon ÷ price. €40 ÷ €960 = 4.17 %.
• **YTM:** everything you earn up to maturity, counting the price difference. It's the one to use for comparisons.

And to know whether you're gaining purchasing power, subtract inflation.
steps.key: YTM is what a bond returns if you hold it to maturity and the issuer pays.
steps.tip: Compare bonds by their YTM, not by their coupon.

u9l3.title: When rates go up, bonds go down

texts: The seesaw
You hold a **€1,000** bond paying 2 % over 10 years, and new ones pay 2 % too. What if rates go up?
Rates rise and new bonds start paying 4 %. What happens to the price of yours?
Nothing: the coupon is fixed
It falls
It rises
Nobody pays €1,000 for 2 % when new ones give 4 %: your bond drops to about **€838**, 16 % less.
With rates at 4 %, stretch the term to 30 years.
**Rates up, price down.** And the longer the bond, the more it moves: with the same rise, a 1-year bond falls 2 % and a 30-year one, 35 %. That sensitivity is called **duration**.
A third gone! Long bonds are the ones that suffer most.
New ones pay more: yours has to get cheaper.
If rates fall, your bond is worth more.
Raise the market interest rate
Quoted at 82
Ana
2021: Ana buys a 10-year government bond with a 1 % coupon.
2023: rates have gone up. New ones pay 3.5 % and hers is quoted at 82.
My «safe» bond is worth 18 % less! I don't need the money, but it's stressing me out.
What do you tell her?
Sell it now, before it falls further
Selling at 82 turns the 18 % drop into a real loss.
If you don't need the money, you can hold it to maturity
If the issuer pays, she gets **100 %** back at the end. Mind you, only at 1 %.
Wait for rates to come down
Nobody controls rates. Better to decide based on her plan than on guessing them.
A rate rise is only a loss if you sell early or there's a default.

steps.title: 2022, the year bonds fell
steps.body:
**Duration** measures how much the price moves when rates change:

**Price change ≈ − duration × change in rates.**

With a duration of 7, if rates rise 1 point, the bond falls roughly 7 %. In 2022 inflation sent rates soaring and many long-term bond indices fell more than 20 %.
steps.key: Rates up, bonds down; the longer the bond, the harder the hit.
steps.tip: Bonds and rates sit on opposite ends of a seesaw.

texts: The issuer's grade
The agencies **S&P, Moody's and Fitch** grade the ability of governments and companies to pay, from AAA to D. Sort each rating.
Investment grade
Speculative
Default
AAA
Top quality: the most reliable issuer.
BB+
Just below BBB−: it's already high yield, or a «junk bond».
A
Investment grade: a good ability to pay.
D
D is the rating for an issuer that has already stopped paying.
BBB−
The last step of investment grade: the dividing line.
CCC
Highly speculative: the risk of not getting paid is high.
Sort all six ratings.
The dividing line is **BBB−**: above it, investment grade; below it, speculative (*high yield*). The worse the rating, the bigger the coupon… and **the higher the risk of not getting paid**.
Hint: the dividing line is BBB−.
Sort each rating
The 14 % bond
Leo
I've found a company bond that pays 14 % a year.
It's like a deposit, only better. I'm putting all my savings into it!
The company has a CCC rating.
What do you tell him?
Great: the coupon is fixed
Fixed, if the company can pay it. With CCC, the risk of default is sky-high.
That 14 % is the price of a high risk of not getting paid
Exactly! Spain's deposit guarantee scheme (FGD) covers deposits, not bonds. A junk bond may pay back almost nothing.
Put in only half your savings
Better, but it's still a huge amount in a single, very risky issuer.
If a bond pays far more than the rest, ask yourself what the market is afraid of.

steps.title: When they don't pay
steps.body:
Anyone lending to a lower-rated borrower demands more interest. The gap compared with a very safe bond is called the **risk premium**; in Spain, it's the gap with the 10-year German bond.

In 2012, Greece's private creditors accepted a haircut of more than half the face value of their bonds. A bankrupt company may pay back almost nothing. That's why you diversify in fixed income too.
steps.key: The rating measures default risk: the worse the rating, the bigger the coupon and the higher the risk of losing.
steps.tip: A very high coupon isn't a gift: it's the price of the risk of not getting paid.

texts: Bill or deposit?
Two places for money you'll need soon: a **Treasury bill** or a **fixed-term deposit** at a bank. Which one does each feature belong to?
Treasury bill
Fixed-term deposit
You pay €980 and get €1,000 at maturity
Bills don't pay a coupon: they're bought at a discount and those €20 are your interest.
Covered by the FGD up to €100,000
The Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (Spain's deposit guarantee scheme) covers up to €100,000 per holder and per bank.
Terms of 3, 6, 9 or 12 months
Bills are government debt for a year or less.
Backed by the state itself
Bills aren't covered by the FGD: their guarantee is the state.
If you take the money out early, there may be a penalty
You leave the money in the bank for a set term, at an agreed rate.
Bought at Treasury auctions, from €1,000
Directly or through your bank or broker.
Sort all six features.
Bills are bought **at a discount** and backed by the state; deposits are covered by the **FGD** up to €100,000 per holder and per bank.
Hint: does the state owe it to you, or a bank?
Sort each feature
Saving for a flat
Laura
I've got €15,000 for the deposit on a flat. I sign in 10 months.
My cousin says I'd make way more on the stock market.
What do you recommend?
Shares, so it grows more
In 10 months the market could drop 20 % right when she needs the money.
A Treasury bill or fixed-term deposit that matures before she signs
Nice! Low risk, and the money will be there on the day she signs.
Leave it in her account at 0 %
It's safe, but she's giving up almost risk-free interest.
And what if my bank went bust?
The FGD covers up to €100,000 per holder and per bank: her €15,000 would be covered.

steps.title: How to compare
steps.body:
Always compare the **annual** return (APR or YTM) after fees. Interest from bills and deposits is taxed in the savings income band (from 19 %).

Neither will make you rich: they're for money you'll need soon.
steps.key: Bills and deposits: low risk and low return, for the short term.
steps.tip: Above €100,000 in one bank, spread it across several banks.

texts: What if inflation takes off?
Think of a regular bond as an account that pays a fixed **3 %** for 10 years. An inflation-linked one pays **1 %** plus inflation.
The regular one gives 3 %; the linked one, 1 % plus inflation. At what inflation rate do they draw level?
At 1 %
At 2 %
At 4 %
With 2 % inflation, the linked one gives 1 + 2 = 3 %, the same as the regular one. That's the **breakeven inflation** the market expects.
Push inflation up until the regular bond yields less than 1 % real.
If inflation beats breakeven (here, **2 %**), the linked bond wins: it keeps giving its 1 % real if you hold it to the end. If inflation stays below, the regular one wins.
Now the regular bond is losing purchasing power.
The linked one, with its 1 % real, now beats the regular one.
Turn inflation up bit by bit
Protected… from everything?
Marta
2021. Marta buys an inflation-linked bond fund «to protect herself».
2022. Inflation takes off… and her fund falls.
I don't get it! I bought it precisely for this.
What happened?
The fund is a scam
No. These bonds also fall in price when real rates go up.
Rates went up and that outweighed the inflation adjustment
Exactly! They protect purchasing power to maturity, but their price moves.
Inflation sinks linked bonds
The opposite: the adjustment helps them. What weighed on them was the rate rise.
A fund sells bonds before maturity: that's why it really does feel rate rises.

steps.title: How they work
steps.body:
The bond adjusts its **face value** for inflation: at 3 %, a €1,000 face value becomes €1,030 and the coupon is calculated on that figure. The Spanish Treasury links them to **eurozone** inflation (excluding tobacco); in the US they're called **TIPS**.

They don't protect you from rate rises if you sell early, or from a default. And if inflation turns out low, they return less than a regular bond.
steps.key: They protect against unexpected inflation if you hold them to the end, not against everything.
steps.tip: No asset protects against everything: each one covers a specific risk.

u9l1-1.prompt: What do you get when you buy a bond?
options: Regular interest and your money back at maturity
A share of the company and voting rights
A dividend decided by the shareholders' meeting
u9l1-1.explanation: A bond is a loan: a coupon while it lasts and the face value at the end.

u9l1-4.prompt: Match each Spanish Treasury security to its term.
u9l1-4.explanation: All three are government debt; what changes is the term.

u9l1-6.prompt: Being called fixed income means its market price never changes.
u9l1-6.explanation: The coupon is fixed; the bond's price moves every day with interest rates and with confidence in the issuer.

u9l1-8.prompt: The regular interest a bond pays is called the ____.
u9l1-8.explanation: The name comes from old paper bonds, which had cut-out coupons you handed in to collect each payment.

options: They give predictable income and usually cushion stock-market falls
You can't possibly lose money on them
They're useless, only shares make money
u9l1-10.explanation: Bonds bring income and stability, although no protection works every time.
feedback: That's it! Though not always: in 2022 they fell at the same time as shares.
If the issuer doesn't pay, or if you sell after they've dropped, you can lose money.
Shares tend to return more over the long run, but bonds give predictable income and usually cushion falls.

u9l2-1.prompt: A bond with a face value of €1,000 is quoted «at 96». How much do you pay for it?

u9l2-2.prompt: A €1,000 bond with a 5 % coupon matures in one year. You buy it at €1,000. What is its YTM?
u9l2-2.explanation: You receive €50 and get back what you paid: 50 ÷ 1,000 = 5 %. If you buy at 100, the YTM equals the coupon.

u9l2-4.prompt: A €1,000 bond with a 5 % coupon matures in one year. You buy it at €1,050. How much do you make in total at maturity?
u9l2-4.explanation: €50 coupon − €50 you lose by receiving €1,000 for something you paid €1,050 for = €0. A YTM of 0 %, even though the coupon is 5 %.

u9l2-5.prompt: If you buy a bond below its face value, its YTM is ____ its coupon.
u9l2-5.explanation: On top of the coupon, at maturity you get more than you paid.

u9l2-6.prompt: Which yield do you use to compare two bonds with different prices and terms?
u9l2-6.explanation: YTM sums up coupons and the price difference to maturity in a single number.

u9l2-7.prompt: Match each concept to what it measures.
u9l2-7.explanation: Coupon, current yield and YTM only match if you buy at exactly 100.
right: Everything you earn up to maturity

u9l2-10.prompt: A bond has a YTM of 3 % and inflation is 2 %. What is its approximate real return?
u9l2-10.explanation: 3 − 2 = 1 %. YTM is nominal: subtract inflation to see whether you're gaining purchasing power.

u9l3-1.prompt: January 2022: US inflation is at a nearly 40-year high and the Federal Reserve is expected to raise rates. This is an ETF of US Treasury bonds with over 20 years to maturity. What did it do next?
u9l3-1.explanation: Very long-term bonds have high duration: their price is very sensitive to rate changes, in both directions.

u9l3-3.prompt: A bond has a duration of 7 and rates rise 1 point. Roughly how much does its price fall?

u9l3-4.prompt: You have €10,000 in bonds with a duration of 6 and rates rise 2 points. Roughly how many euros do you lose?

u9l3-5.prompt: A bond with a duration of 8, and rates fall 1.5 points. Roughly how much does its price rise?
u9l3-5.explanation: 8 × 1.5 = a 12 % rise: the seesaw works upwards too.

u9l3-6.prompt: Order from least to most sensitive to interest rates.
u9l3-6.explanation: The longer the term, the higher the duration: the 30-year one moves the most.

u9l3-10.prompt: Match each situation to what usually happens.
u9l3-10.explanation: It's the seesaw rule, plus the role of duration and term.
right: You get what was agreed if the issuer pays

u9l4-1.prompt: Match each rating to its meaning.
u9l4-1.explanation: Above BBB− is investment grade; below it, speculative.

u9l4-2.prompt: Order from best to worst rating.
u9l4-2.explanation: Quality drops through the letters from AAA down to D (default).

u9l4-3.prompt: Why does a high-yield bond pay more interest?
options: Because the issuer is more generous
Because the risk of default is higher
u9l4-3.explanation: Anyone lending to a riskier issuer demands more interest in return.

u9l4-7.prompt: The difference between what the Spanish 10-year bond pays and the German one is called the ____.
u9l4-7.explanation: It measures how much more the market demands for lending to Spain than to Germany.

u9l4-8.prompt: Which organisations rate the debt of governments and companies? Select all.
u9l4-8.explanation: The CNMV supervises the markets in Spain, but it doesn't rate issuers.

u9l4-9.prompt: For the same term, a German bond pays 2.5 % and a Spanish one 3.2 %. What is the risk premium in basis points? (1 point = 100 bp)

u9l5-1.prompt: You buy a 12-month bill for €980 and at maturity you receive €1,000. What return do you get? (two decimal places)

u9l5-2.prompt: A €10,000 deposit at 2.5 % APR for one year. With 19 % withheld in tax, how much do you make net?

u9l5-3.prompt: You have €130,000 in a deposit at a single bank. If the bank goes bust, how much falls outside the deposit guarantee scheme (FGD)?
u9l5-3.explanation: It covers up to €100,000 per holder and per bank: 130,000 − 100,000 = €30,000 uncovered.

u9l5-5.prompt: What terms does the Spanish Treasury issue bills at?
u9l5-5.explanation: Bills are always one year or less.

u9l5-7.prompt: Which time horizon does each product suit best?
options: Monthly contribution to a global ETF
u9l5-7.explanation: For the short term, safety comes first; over decades, long-term returns matter more than the ups and downs.
right: Money I'll need in under 1 year

u9l5-10.prompt: Spanish Treasury bills can be bought from ____ €.
u9l5-10.explanation: It's the minimum amount at Treasury auctions.

u9l6-1.prompt: An inflation-linked bond with a face value of €1,000. This year inflation is 3 %. What is the new face value?

u9l6-2.prompt: That bond pays a 1 % real coupon on the adjusted face value of €1,030. How much do you receive this year? (two decimal places)

u9l6-4.prompt: When does the inflation-linked bond beat the regular one?
options: If inflation ends up higher than the market expected
u9l6-4.explanation: If inflation beats breakeven, the face-value adjustment more than makes up for its lower coupon.

u9l6-6.prompt: Spanish Treasury inflation-linked bonds are adjusted using eurozone inflation.
u9l6-6.explanation: They use the eurozone harmonised index of consumer prices excluding tobacco, not the Spanish CPI.

u9l6-8.prompt: An inflation-linked bond held to maturity: does it protect you or not?
options: A rate rise if you have to sell early
u9l6-8.explanation: It covers inflation risk; not rate risk if you sell early, nor credit risk.

options: They protect against unexpected inflation if you hold them to the end, but their price moves too
No, they don't protect from anything
u9l6-10.explanation: Each asset covers a specific risk; none covers them all.
feedback: Nice! They cover a specific risk, not all of them.
They protect against inflation, not against rate rises or a default.
They do protect purchasing power if you hold them to maturity.
